J0269981369:
Seven woven tapestries, developed with the TextielMuseum Tilburg, depict events from the Battle of Karbala, while exploring beauty as it unfolds through the many forms of Islamic art, with a focus on abstraction through saturation. Islamic art emphasises inwardness and abstraction, resisting representation, but what exactly is abstraction? Arabic has no single word for it. The closest are التجريد (al-tajrīd), to strip away in search of the essence, and الروحانية (al-rūḥāniyya), to feel through the soul as a sensory way of experiencing.

Abstraction is then not only a visual method but a way to reach the divine. Rūḥāniyya is not an abstract spirituality but a felt presence rooted in the Heart (Qalb), the centre of perception, intention and divine encounter in Islamic thought. The installation reflects on words spoken by Saida Zaynab (a.s.), who, after the Battle of Karbala and the martyrdom of her family, was ridiculed by her oppressors and asked, “How did you experience the death of your family?” She replied:

I saw nothing but beauty.

Her brother Hussein ibn Ali (a.s.) was murdered, decapitated, and his body mutilated. Yet her words, spoken in the face of unimaginable cruelty, resonate across centuries. The beauty she saw lies beyond the physical realm and its events. In the Battle of Karbala and the martyrdom of her family she saw unwavering faith in the face of agony and injustice, a testimony to the prevalence of ultimate justice and truth.
E4217115539:
The three tapestries in the series deal with two myths about the Sumerian moon goddess Inanna, who represents love, fertility and prosperity, but is also described as warlike and addicted to conquest. The outer carpets tell of Inanna’s descent into the underworld. To get there, she must lay aside all her divine instruments of power at seven gates. Naked and powerless, she finally stands before Ereškigal, goddess of the underworld. Although Inanna succeeds in pushing Ereškigal from her throne, she is sentenced to death. While her lifeless body hangs on a hook in the underworld, fertility disappears from the world. Inanna’s helper then asks Enki, god of wisdom, for help. After incantations and rituals, Ereškigal relents, releases Inanna’s body and brings her back to life. In exchange, Inanna’s husband must take her place in the underworld.

The middle carpet is dedicated to the myth of Inanna and the Huluppu tree, which is sometimes equated with the tree of life and world tree of Eridu in Mesopotamian cosmology. Its roots reach the underworld, its crown touches the sky and houses the sun. Inanna found the tree uprooted by a storm and planted it in her garden. When she wanted to cut it down to build a bed and a throne, she found she could not, because mythical beings had nested in it: the Anzu bird, the ghost girl Lilith and the unenchantable snake. Finally the hero Gilgamesh offers his help, drives the beings away and fells the tree so that Inanna can fulfil her wishes. This is followed by the story of another descent into the underworld, by Gilgamesh’s friend and companion Enkidu.

The tapestries ask for patient looking. Motif by motif, ornament by ornament, they open onto layers of ancient pictorial worlds that tell of descent, change and return in cyclical repetitions and symmetries. The work is shown together with a poem by the artist and writer Etel Adnan (1925–2021), which takes up the same motifs of destruction, hell and rebirth.
X2570966268:
Archaeological and philological theories, which try to reconcile the mythical places of religious traditions with the geographical experience of mankind, locate the earthly Garden of Eden in Mesopotamia. GARDEN_OF_EDEN.PNG builds on this, as the video installation GARDEN_OF_EDEN.ISO (2023) did before it. The tapestry was created on a modern Jacquard loom at the TextielMuseum in Tilburg. It unites motifs and ornaments from a long iconographic research in a non-hierarchical, symmetrical order, from antiquity, to Islamic traditions, to contemporary computer graphics. Among them are gods, heroic figures and chimeric creatures from mythology such as Enki and Anzu, and Gilgamesh and Enkidu. Above and below, they are framed by the Euphrates and the Tigris.

The work carries a futuristic vision, using materials historically connected to digital media: hologram, digital language and tapestry. Grown out of research into family history and questions of displacement, it borrows the storytelling of the almost vanished carpet- and tapestry-making of southern Iraq, and through digitising and machine production it re-creates new, imagined stories. Its signs and symbols stem from contemporary popular culture and early digital games as much as from Mesopotamian symbols and characters, reinterpreted and placed in the context of the contemporary moment in Iraq, opening paths to imagining the future. Carpets, traditionally made for storytelling, have reflected history for centuries, often showing the glory of a culture. What could carpets tell today, if asked? What would their signs and symbols be, if left to their own devices in the contemporary moment?
H3576209373: A Jacquard-knitted cotton tapestry wrapped around a foil body and shown lying on the floor. The work is dedicated to Fatima (s.a.), mother of Zaynab, Hussein and Abbas. At its centre a radiant figure opens up in white against the black knit, its light spreading through the surrounding pattern. Because the knit follows the shape beneath it, the tapestry becomes a body rather than a surface on a wall.
Z1653523331: A figure in an abaya spins yarn with a spindle, surrounded by Ahwari symbols. Grandma (Creation) is a tribute to a grandmother who threaded yarn for southern Iraqi tapestries, in a family that has worked in carpet production for generations. The act of spinning is inseparable from the act of making the world.
B3229528212:
Huriya (حرية) is the Arabic word for freedom. The title, Huriya, Huriya, Huriya, Huriya, comes from a chant heard at protests all over the world.

The design is based on the keffiyeh, a cloth of Iraqi origin: its name is traced to Kufa, the city in southern Iraq. Each of its patterns carries a meaning. The fishnet speaks of fishermen and of the bond with the water, the olive leaves of resilience and of being rooted in the land, and the bold bands of the trade routes that crossed the region. The flag redraws these patterns pixel by pixel, joining the history of early computer graphics with carpet-making, and takes its proportions from a keffiyeh kept at home. It can be hung both vertically and horizontally; the design leaves room for that freedom.

The flag was inaugurated on 12 September 2024 with a performative guided tour together with Yasmina Reggad, performance artist, dramaturge, writer and researcher. Walking from Cas-co with the flag, and with the chant as the one constant, the tour ended at the flagpole, where the flag was hoisted. A fundraiser with risograph prints that evening supported Brussels for Palestine.
B0282079059:
GARDEN_OF_EDEN.ISO works as a manipulated, beautiful recollection rooted in a PlayStation 1 memory card and in lived experience: a digital iteration of an emotional atemporality.

It starts from a home in Iraq saturated with carpet patterns, in a family of generations of workers in the trade and logistics of carpet-making. Stepping into the living room felt like entering a sanctuary filled with chains and chains of motifs derived from Eden, where one softly takes comfort. Woven patterns clung to the walls providing warmth, unfurled on the floors providing comfort, covered the diwan extending shelter, and silk-like tapestries graced the ceiling, as if inviting one to drift through the infinite world they create while unfolding beauty. On the floor before the TV, Legend of Mana played on the PlayStation, and fragments of the knotted carpets whispered through the game’s pixels like the woven threads all around, blending reality and virtuality. Everything slowly danced, so wonderfully.

The work is another iteration of a long research into Southern Iraqi carpets, woven by the Marsh Arabs in the Mesopotamian marshes of Iraq. These carpets are unique and different from any other textile tradition in the Middle East: flowers, animals, human figures, symbols and geometric motifs are embroidered with wool yarn on a hand-woven ground.
W0066330841:
In non-Western contexts carpets aren’t simply a delimitation of a space or a decoration; their function is equally holistic and spiritual. Here carpets are central to a story of displacement and migration from Iraq to Antwerp, and become a spatial representation of Arab identity. The work counters the dominance of Western ‘universal design’ through research into Southern Iraqi woven carpets, whose long history has been almost completely erased by the country’s colonial, patriarchal and dictatorial past.

Garden of Eden is a first physical carpet, made in collaboration with TextielLab in Tilburg. It encompasses many of the tools encountered in that research: multi-centred perspectives leading to a harmonious whole without hierarchy; geometric ornamentation and arabesque symmetry, as present in Iraqi material culture and in Islamic art; symbols of a diasporic locality such as reeds, water buffalo and fish; and the pixel, as a way to embrace vital connections between old and new.
O4271602504:
Bluest River grew out of research carried out during an advanced master’s programme in 2021–2022, a return to more material ways of making and to the relational situations that could constitute the production of printed carpets.

The tradition of hand printing with wooden blocks dates back hundreds of years and was originally an Indian technique for printing on silk. It was used across the Levant and its neighbouring countries, but in most areas was replaced by machines. Now, through the machine, it is revived. Working with the machine, intricate symbols are drawn from the visual culture present in Iraq and laser cut into durable, usable wooden stamps. Each stamp-object recalls symbols recurrent in southern Iraqi tapestries. The stamps were used to create Bluest River, but are also meant to be shared in performances and workshops as an artistic tool for passing on knowledge of crafts and cultural heritage: talking about old technologies through new ones. Bluest River is a step further in developing ways of sharing research. Made collaboratively with Sadrie Alves.
S1843187038:
This work acts as a paradox in the spacetime continuum: an apparent overlapping of different time periods and an odd connection to other localities. It is both a channelling and a reinterpretation. It is both an indignation and a gratification. It can both curse and comfort.

A temporal rift reveals Inanna’s altar in the year 3XXX BC, in the region now known as Iraq, as a constellation of video imagery. The videos show interpretations of Inanna, goddess of war and love, and her priests. The altar is envisioned as an audio-visual-sculptural space that submerges viewers in poetic projections: a speculative and transformative stream of significant gestures enacted by Inanna, who performs a ritualistic dance of prayer, remembrance and grievance, surrounded by her spiralling followers.

The work is inspired by Saidiya Hartman’s critical fabulation. “Fabula” signifies a potentiality that can lead towards a kind of historical speculation, or “critical fabulation,” as she puts it, in which one could “present an impossible tale” while simultaneously emphasising the “impossibility of its telling.” It can both affirm and criticise.

The work is a gateway to an encounter with a parallel reality, in which these priests and their rites were not colonised, marginalised or forcefully erased: a reality where these ancient spiritual practices had their fair chance of developing, transforming and transcending to heights beyond the confines of our current collective comprehension.
T3048144612:
Weaving pixels into threads of past memories, the work explores the intricate relationship between rivers and textiles in the Mesopotamian marshes of Iraq, and the possibility of transforming the imagery of Iraqi tapestries into a film. The film is split into four chapters, or symbols; each symbol represents the video imagery behind it. Some of the footage was filmed and sent by family members living in southern Iraq. Other footage was extracted from online video sharing websites and social media platforms.

The work transcends several geographies, Iraq, Belgium and the virtual, becoming a digital conversation with and through the carpet. Each symbol is complemented by an Iraqi song that portrays its meaning, while also touching on migration, feelings of yearning and the act of remembrance.
